content.user_title: Plan A/B Tests and Interpret Experiment Results
content.value_statement: Poorly designed experiments can produce misleading results and waste traffic. This skill guides hypothesis design, sample planning, metric selection, and documented decisions.
actual_capabilities: Structure test hypotheses around observations, proposed changes, audiences, and measurable outcomes.
Estimate sample requirements and collection duration using reference tables, traffic, exposure, and allocation.
Define primary, secondary, and guardrail metrics for experiment plans.
Compare A/B, A/B/n, multivariate, and split-URL designs with their traffic requirements.
Guide interpretation of effect sizes, confidence intervals, p-values, and planned stopping rules.
Draft test plans, results records, stakeholder updates, and ICE-prioritized experiment backlogs.
limitations: Provides instructions and templates, not an executable experimentation platform or statistical engine.
Does not deploy variants, configure analytics, or collect production data automatically.
Sample-size tables are approximate; exact calculations require suitable calculators and declared assumptions.
Requires reliable user-supplied traffic, baseline rates, experiment results, and business constraints.

use_cases.title: Prepare a conversion experiment
use_cases.description: Turn a proposed headline change into a hypothesis, metric plan, traffic split, sample estimate, and launch checklist.

use_cases.title: Review a completed product test
use_cases.description: Assess a completed experiment using effect estimates, uncertainty, guardrails, and the original stopping rule before recommending rollout.

use_cases.title: Organize an experimentation program
use_cases.description: Prioritize hypotheses with ICE scoring and establish review schedules, documentation templates, and an experiment playbook.

prompt_templates.title: Frame a first test
prompt_templates.prompt: Help me plan an A/B test for [page] comparing [current version] with [proposed change]. Ask for missing baseline, traffic, and business goals.
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner: clarify a test idea before implementation.

prompt_templates.title: Estimate sample and duration
prompt_templates.prompt: Plan a two-arm test with [baseline]% conversion, [daily traffic] eligible users, [exposure]% exposure, and [relative MDE]% lift. Estimate samples and duration. State allocation, power, significance level, and business-cycle assumptions.
prompt_templates.scenario: Intermediate: check whether traffic supports the planned test.

prompt_templates.title: Interpret completed results
prompt_templates.prompt: Review this completed fixed-horizon test: [counts per arm], [planned sample], [primary metric], and [guardrails]. Report effect size, uncertainty, assumptions, and practical impact. Respect the original stopping rule and label unplanned segments exploratory.
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced: prepare an evidence-based rollout recommendation.

prompt_templates.title: Build an experiment program
prompt_templates.prompt: Build an experimentation program for [product] using [traffic], [team capacity], and [backlog]. Prioritize ideas with ICE scores, stating assumptions. Define test plans, guardrails, review cadence, and playbook entries. Explain how exposure and multiple variants affect feasibility.
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced: coordinate a repeatable team experimentation process.

output_examples.input: Our baseline conversion is 5%. We want to detect a 20% relative lift with 1,000 eligible users daily and full exposure.
output: Design: two variants with 50/50 allocation, 5% significance level, and 80% power.
Target: 5% to 6% conversion, a one-percentage-point absolute increase.
Reference estimate: approximately 8,200 users per variant, or 16,400 total.
Collection estimate: 17 days, rounded up from 16.4 days. Schedule analysis after the planned collection period and required business cycles.
Confirm the exact sample with a suitable calculator before launch.

output_examples.input: Variant B shows p = 0.04 and a 2% relative lift at the planned endpoint, but refunds increased. Should we ship?
output: The result meets a preselected 0.05 threshold only under the planned analysis assumptions.
A p-value of 0.04 does not mean a 96% probability that the change works.
Review the effect interval and refund guardrail before rollout.
Do not approve rollout from statistical significance alone; compare conversion gains with refund costs.

best_practices: Define the primary metric, minimum detectable effect, sample target, and stopping rule before launch.
Verify tracking and stable variant assignment, then monitor technical failures and guardrail metrics.
Document effect sizes, uncertainty, business impact, and follow-up hypotheses for every completed test.
anti_patterns: Stop a fixed-horizon test early because an interim result appears significant.
Change variants or select favorable segments after reviewing results without labeling the analysis exploratory.
Treat statistical significance as sufficient evidence of business value while ignoring guardrail harm.

faq.question: What information should I provide?
faq.answer: Provide the proposed change, baseline conversion, eligible traffic, minimum worthwhile lift, available tools, and business constraints.

faq.question: Does the skill run experiments automatically?
faq.answer: No. It supplies planning and analysis guidance. You must implement variants, configure tracking, and collect results through your own tools.

faq.question: Can I use it with Claude and Codex?
faq.answer: The skill supports Claude, Codex, and Claude Code. It consists of Markdown instructions and reference materials.

faq.question: Are the sample-size estimates exact?
faq.answer: No. Reference tables provide rounded estimates under stated assumptions. Confirm exact requirements with a suitable calculator, especially for unequal allocation or multiple comparisons.

faq.question: Can I stop as soon as results become significant?
faq.answer: Not for a fixed-horizon test. Follow its planned stopping rule. Early stopping requires an appropriate predefined method, except for safety-related guardrail stops.

faq.question: Can it help when traffic is low?
faq.answer: Yes. It helps assess feasibility and consider fewer variants, larger detectable effects, or qualitative alternatives without claiming stronger evidence than available.
